target_audience: High school students and geometry enthusiasts

outline.target_audience: High school students and geometry enthusiasts

sections.title: Foundation: The Ladder of Dimensions
sections.content: Introduction to the concept of dimensions (0D to 3D) through the 'Sweep' method. A point (0D) moves to create a line (1D); a line moves to create a plane (2D); a plane moves to create a volume (3D). This establishes the prerequisite understanding of how one dimension generates the next.
sections.example: Visualize a tiny glowing firefly. As it moves in a straight line, it leaves a trail of light (1D). If that line slides sideways, it creates a glowing ribbon (2D). If the ribbon lifts upward, it forms a glowing box (3D).

sections.title: The Shadow Puzzle: 3D to 2D Projection
sections.content: Explaining 'Projection'—how high-dimensional objects lose information when viewed in lower dimensions. This is a critical skill for solving spatial reasoning puzzles where you must identify an object based on its 'footprint'.
sections.example: A rotating wireframe cube is placed in front of a light source. Depending on its orientation, its 2D shadow can look like a square, a rectangle, or even a regular hexagon. The 'puzzle' is guessing the 3D shape just from the shifting shadow.

sections.title: The Slicing Puzzle: Cross-Sectional Logic
sections.content: Introducing 'Slicing'—the intersection of a 3D object and a 2D plane. This teaches students to visualize internal geometry and understand that a single 3D object can produce multiple 2D shapes depending on the angle of the cut.
sections.example: A 'Magic Chef' slices a solid orange cone. If they slice parallel to the base, the cross-section is a circle. If they slice diagonally, it's an ellipse. If they slice through the tip, it's a triangle. The puzzle asks: 'What shape must I cut to get a parabola?'

sections.title: The Unfolding Puzzle: Nets and Topography
sections.content: Focusing on 'Nets'—flattening 3D surfaces into 2D maps. This section explores the relationship between vertices, edges, and faces when a shape is 'broken' and laid flat, which is essential for origami-based geometry puzzles.
sections.example: A flat 'Paper Robot' character wants to turn into a cube. We show 11 different 2D arrangements of six squares (nets). The puzzle is to identify which 2D layout can successfully fold into the robot's 3D body without overlapping edges.

sections.title: The Ultimate Leap: Visualizing the 4th Dimension
sections.content: Applying the previous logic (Shadows and Slicing) to the Tesseract (4D Hypercube). By using analogy—as a 2D shadow is to a 3D cube, a 3D 'shadow' is to a 4D cube—we bridge the gap to higher-dimensional thinking.
sections.example: An animated 'Hyper-Spider' crawls through a Tesseract. To us 3D beings, the spider appears to grow, shrink, and vanish as it moves through the 4D space, similar to how a 3D sphere looks like a growing and shrinking circle to a 2D 'Flatlander'.

storyboard.title: Foundation: The Ladder of Dimensions
lecture_lines: A zero-dimensional point has no size or direction.
Dragging a point creates a one-dimensional line.
Shifting a line sideways produces a two-dimensional plane.
Moving a plane upward builds a three-dimensional volume.
Each shift adds a new direction to our space.
animations: A bright white dot (#FFFFFF) appears in the center.
The dot moves right, leaving a golden trail (#FFD700) forming a line.
The line sweeps upward, stretching into a sky blue rectangle (#00BFFF).
The rectangle expands outward in perspective, forming an orange cube (#FF4500).
Highlight three axes: Red (X), Green (Y), and Blue (Z).

storyboard.title: The Shadow Puzzle: 3D to 2D Projection
lecture_lines: Higher dimensions lose information when projected onto lower ones.
A cube's 2D shadow changes shape as it rotates.
We can identify objects by studying their shifting footprints.
animations: A white wireframe cube (#FFFFFF) rotates on the left side.
A gray shadow (#808080) is projected onto a 2D plane on the right.
As the cube rotates, the shadow transforms from a square to a hexagon.

storyboard.title: The Slicing Puzzle: Cross-Sectional Logic
lecture_lines: Slicing reveals the internal shapes hidden within three dimensions.
A flat plane cuts horizontally through our solid cone.
This creates a circle where the two surfaces intersect.
Tilting the plane produces an elongated elliptical shape.
Slicing through the tip exposes a sharp triangle.
animations: Show a transparent orange cone (#FFA500) against the black background.
A bright green plane (#00FF00) slices horizontally through the cone.
Highlight the circular edge of the horizontal cross-section.
Tilt the green plane to a diagonal angle, showing an ellipse.
Rotate the plane vertically through the tip to show a triangle.

storyboard.title: The Unfolding Puzzle: Nets and Topography
lecture_lines: Nets flatten 3D surfaces into 2D paper maps.
Folding these maps reconstructs the original geometric solid.
Many patterns exist, but only some form a cube.
animations: A pink T-shaped net of six squares (#FF69B4) lies flat.
The squares rotate and fold together to form a solid 3D cube.
A faulty net arrangement appears; squares overlap when folding, showing it fails.

storyboard.title: The Ultimate Leap: Visualizing the 4th Dimension
lecture_lines: A tesseract is the four-dimensional version of a cube.
We visualize it through 3D projections and cross-sections.
As it moves, it appears to turn inside out.
Higher dimensions follow the same logic as lower ones.
Geometry puzzles help us decode these complex unseen worlds.
animations: Display a white wireframe Tesseract (#FFFFFF) as a cube within a cube.
The Tesseract rotates, showing its inner and outer cubes swapping places.
Show a golden sphere (#FFD700) passing through a 2D plane.
The sphere appears as a circle that grows and then shrinks.
Illustrate the analogy: 4D objects appear as 3D cross-sections to us.
